title: Modeling Time and History | Insightful Data Lab
description:
The first two come from stream processing, where the distinction is unavoidable and has been stated precisely. The Dataflow Model paper defines **event time** as “the time at which the event itself actually occurred, i.e. a record of system clock time (for whatever system generated the event) at the time of occurrence,” and **processing time** as “the time at which an event is observed at any given point during processing within the pipeline, i.e. the current time according to the system clock.” The paper is explicit that it makes no assumptions about clock synchronization between the two.
The asymmetry between them is what makes the distinction load-bearing: event time for a given event essentially never changes, while processing time changes constantly for each event as it moves through the pipeline. The gap is not a defect to be engineered away either — communication delays, scheduling, time spent processing, and pipeline serialization produce what the paper calls “an inherent and dynamically changing amount of skew between the two domains.”
The third clock comes from the business rather than the plumbing. An event can occur on one date, be recorded on another, and take effect on a third: a contract signed in March, entered in April, effective from January. Call this **effective time** — the period for which a fact is true as far as the business is concerned. Martin Fowler’s treatment of [bitemporal history](https://insightful-data-lab.com/2024/09/27/valid-time-and-system-time/) frames the pairing well, describing actual history as what “records what history should be given perfect transmission of information,”

| Clock | Answers | Can it change later? | Getting it wrong looks like |
|---|---|---|---|
| Event time | When did this happen in the world? | The event’s actual time does not; a recorded timestamp can be corrected — a wrong time zone or clock — as a tracked revision | Yesterday’s totals keep changing as late data arrives |
| Processing time | When was it handled at a given stage of the pipeline? | It has a different value at every stage and on every retry | Reprocessing moves events into different days |
| Effective time | When is this true, for business purposes? | **Yes** — corrections move it | Retroactive changes silently rewrite closed periods |
Two practical rules follow. The first is to **aggregate on the time axis the question is about, and keep that meaning fixed when data is reprocessed.** A figure for a period — March revenue — usually belongs on event time, so that a re-run cannot move a sale into a different day. Whether something was in force belongs on effective time: the contract signed in March but effective from January counts as active in January. Measures of the pipeline itself, such as throughput or ingestion delay, properly use processing time. How a table is physically partitioned is a separate decision, driven by how it is loaded and pruned; what matters for correctness is that each aggregate uses the right axis and that re-running the pipeline on the same inputs, with the same interpretation of time, cannot change which period a record belongs to. Correcting a timestamp — fixing a time-zone error that put 00:30 UTC on the previous local day, say — can legitimately move an event to another period, but as a recorded revision that keeps the original value and says which periods it affected, not as a side effect of a re-run.

title: How to Model Time in Knowledge Graphs
description:
The simplest approach in a labeled property graph: attach `validFrom` and `validTo` properties directly to the relationship.
```
// Jane's employment with a validity interval
MATCH (j:Person {name:'Jane'}), (a:Company {name:'Acme'})
CREATE (j)-[:WORKS_AT {validFrom: date('2019-03-01'),
validTo: date('2025-06-30'),
role: 'Engineer'}]->(a)
// Who worked at Acme on a given date?
MATCH (p:Person)-[r:WORKS_AT]->(:Company {name:'Acme'})
WHERE r.validFrom <= date('2021-01-01')
AND (r.validTo IS NULL OR r.validTo >= date('2021-01-01'))
RETURN p.name, r.role
```

## Pattern 2: Event / Interval Nodes
When a relationship itself has rich, changing attributes, promote the time-bound fact to its own node. Instead of an edge, you create an **Employment** node connecting Jane and Acme, with its own interval and properties.
```
(j:Person)-[:HAS]->(e:Employment {validFrom:..., validTo:..., role:...})-[:AT]->(a:Company)
```
This reifies the relationship into a first-class entity. It's more verbose but far more flexible — the Employment node can carry salary history, manager links, its own provenance, and multiple sub-relationships. It's the standard pattern when a relationship needs the full richness of an entity, and it handles overlapping concurrent states cleanly because each is simply a separate node. The cost is more nodes and an extra hop in every query that touches the relationship.
## Pattern 3: Reification (RDF)
In classic RDF, a triple can't directly have a fourth element. **Reification** turns the statement into a resource you can annotate:
```
_:stmt rdf:subject :Jane ;
rdf:predicate :worksAt ;
rdf:object :Acme ;
:validFrom "2019-03-01"^^xsd:date ;
:validTo "2025-06-30"^^xsd:date .
```
It's verbose — one statement becomes five triples — but fully standards-compliant and supported everywhere RDF is. Reification was the original RDF answer to metadata-on-triples and is covered in the standards topic earlier in this course. Its verbosity is the main reason a cleaner successor emerged.

Decide early on granularity (dates vs. timestamps with seconds) and always store times in UTC with explicit zone handling at the edges. Temporal bugs frequently come not from the graph model but from mixing local times, forgetting daylight-saving transitions, or comparing a date against a timestamp. Pick one representation and enforce it across every ingestion path.

title: Your Agent Memory Needs Two Clocks
description:
Temporal databases distinguish [application time from system time](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/19/ddl-temporal-tables.html). Application time describes when a row was valid in the domain being modelled. System time describes when that version existed in the database. Keeping both is usually called bitemporal modelling.
The same split is useful for agent memory:
| Clock | Question | Example fields |
|---|---|---|
| Valid time | When did this claim apply in the user's world? | `valid_at`, `invalid_at` |
| Knowledge time | When did the memory system treat the claim as live? | `created_at`, `expired_at` |
Zep's [fact model](https://help.getzep.com/facts) uses those four timestamps. In the Acme example, the employment claim has a valid interval from April 1 to June 30 and a knowledge interval from April 10 to July 26.

A flat vector store offers two tempting update strategies. Overwriting the old chunk makes current retrieval cleaner but destroys historical answers. Appending the correction preserves history but leaves two semantically similar chunks competing for retrieval.
A bitemporal write keeps both records and changes their roles. When the July message arrives, the memory system can:
1. Link the new message to the existing employment claim.
2. Set the old claim's `invalid_at` to June 30.
3. Set its `expired_at` to July 26, when the correction became known.
4. Preserve both source messages as provenance.
[Graphiti](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti), the temporal knowledge graph behind Zep, separates episodes from extracted facts and attaches validity windows to relationships. The episode keeps the original source material; the relationship can be invalidated without deleting that source.

title: What Is a Bi-Temporal Knowledge Graph? (and Why AI Memory Needs One)
description:
- A bi-temporal knowledge graph tracks every fact on two clocks instead of one.
- Those clocks are valid time (when a fact was true in the world) and transaction time (when the system learned it).
- One timestamp can't answer both "what is true now" and "what did we believe in March."
- Old facts get invalidated, not deleted, so the full record stays auditable.
- For AI agents, that structure is what stops a model from restating deprecated facts as current.
## What "Bi-Temporal" Actually Means
A bi-temporal data model tracks two independent kinds of time for every fact it stores. Valid time is the period during which a fact is true in the real world. Transaction time is when the system actually recorded that fact. The terms come from Richard Snodgrass and are codified in the [SQL:2011 standard](https://contact-rajeshvinayagam.medium.com/bi-temporal-data-modeling-an-overview-cbba335d1947). Martin Fowler finds those labels confusing and prefers the plainer pair of [actual time and record time](https://martinfowler.com/articles/bitemporal-history.html), which name the same two axes.

A valid-time-only store knows your pricing changed on March 1, but it cannot tell you what the system believed about that price on February 25 when someone made a decision. A transaction-time-only store knows when each record landed, but it cannot represent a backdated correction without overwriting what came before. Either way, you lose the ability to separate what was true from what you thought was true. A bi-temporal model keeps both axes side by side, so every fact carries an answer to two different questions at once.

title: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM Decisions Already Made
description:
Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the mo-

title: Event-Centric Temporal Knowledge Graph Construction: A Survey
description:
reasoning, often overlooking the temporal dimension of events. Given the widespread presence of time-related information, addressing this temporal aspect could potentially enhance the quality of common-sense reasoning within existing knowledge graphs. In this comprehensive survey, we aim to identify and evaluate the key tasks involved in constructing temporal knowledge graphs centered around events. These tasks can be categorized into three main components: (a) event extraction, (b) the extraction of temporal relationships and attributes, and (c) the creation of event-based knowledge graphs and timelines. Our systematic review focuses on the examination of available datasets and language technologies for addressing these tasks.

One particularly important part of events is their timing, as it helps us arrange the events in order of when they happened. The most common way to represent this information is by using knowledge graphs.

For that purpose, we analyzed the properties that are defined in the OWL time ontology ([https://www.w3.org/TR/owl-time/](https://www.w3.org/TR/owl-time/) (accessed on 12 October 2023)), as it is commonly used to record the time in knowledge graphs. The OWL time ontology encapsulates several key time components, including (1) time of the event (date, year, month, day, day of the week, time zone, etc.), (2) duration (years, months, weeks, days, etc.), (3) interval (combination of a time and duration), and (4) temporal relation (before, after, meets, met by, overlaps overlapped by, starts, started by, during, contains, finishes, finished by, and equals).

Event-centric knowledge graphs, like EventKG constructed by Gottschalk [147], focus on events as the central entities. EventKG was created by extracting events from various sources, including Wikidata [2], DBpedia [1], YAGO [3], Wikipedia Event Lists, and Wikipedia Current Events Portal. It comprises 322,669 events with 88,473,111 relations, including information about the time and location of events when available.

title: What is a bitemporal knowledge graph?
description:
Most systems store one timestamp per record: when it was written. That answers “when did this change,” but it can't answer “when did this *become* true” separately from “when did we *find out*.” Those are two different questions, and conflating them is how audit trails quietly lie.
A bitemporal knowledge graph keeps both:
- **Valid time** — the interval during which a fact holds in the real world.
- **Transaction time** — the interval during which the system believed it.
Every fact is a small claim with both stamps. “Acme is on the growth plan” is true *in the world* from March 10, but Brain only *recorded* it on March 12.
## The correction problem
Here is the scenario that breaks single-clock systems. A customer switched plans on March 10. Your system didn't hear about it until March 12.
| | Valid time | Transaction time |
|---|---|---|
| starter | Jan 1 → Mar 10 | Jan 1 → (capped Mar 12) |
| growth | Mar 10 → now | Mar 12 → now |
Now ask: *“On March 11, what plan did we think Acme was on?”*
The honest answer is **starter** — because the switch wasn't recorded until the 12th. A single-clock store can't produce that answer. Once you write the correction, it looks like you always knew. Bitemporal keeps transaction time independent, so replaying March 11 returns what you actually knew on March 11.

In INITE Brain every row carries / and / . A default search resolves the active slice at . Pass and the query re-pins valid time; pass a transaction bound and it re-pins what was known. A correction inserts a new fact and caps the old one's valid interval — the original row stays, so the timeline is never destroyed, only extended.
